prime.problem: A scheduler can place jobs well and still be distrusted: users see ‘PENDING’ with no reason, suspect another team, cancel and resubmit, while dashboards show a busy cluster doing little useful work.
prime.fits: Third case-study card. It builds on the gang-scheduling card (the 64-pod job that can't start with 46 free) and the fair-share card (fair queueing), and on cs-5's lesson that the right metric matters.
expect: utilization vs goodput vs capacity waste
prime.goal: Write a useful pending reason, compute what a utilization histogram says about wasted capacity, and explain what fair queueing moves between users.

attend: Why do 46 free GPUs start zero of a 64-pod job, and what must the pending message include to make that believable?
Which of the five trust dimensions can users only check after the fact, and why?
How can a cluster be 95% allocated while 28% of allocated GPU time does nothing?
What does fair queueing take away from the heavy user, and why is the total waiting unchanged?
When is all this product work unnecessary?

must: A gang job needs every GPU at once → 46 of 64 free still starts 0 pods → a bare PENDING looks like unfairness → a reason with the numbers (needs 64, 46 free, 18 more) and an estimate turns suspicion into understanding
Allocation counts GPUs handed out; busy-ness counts GPUs computing → 28% of allocated time sits at 0% → goodput (work that survives) and capacity waste belong on the dashboard, not allocation alone
FCFS lets whoever floods the queue win → round-robin across users gives each user one slot per round → a light user's wait drops (B1 10 → 1) and the heavy user's last job waits longer (9 → 10)
A preempted job without a checkpoint is busy but lost → FAILED_PREEMPTED turns hours of allocation into zero goodput → SIGTERM-then-checkpoint makes preemption a pause
elevated: An estimate is only as good as the scheduler's view of future arrivals → a higher-priority job can break a promised start → a wrong estimate may cost more trust than none

compress.prompt: From memory, write the pending reason for the 64-pod job, list the five trust dimensions with one user question each, and compute the mean utilization idea in one line (bin midpoints × shares). Then one sentence on why allocation is the wrong headline metric.
checklist: PENDING (gang): needs 64 GPUs, 46 free, waiting for 18 more, plus an estimate
predictability, reason attached, procedural fairness, control, reliability
mean ≈ Σ midpoint × share ≈ 32.9%; 28% of allocated time at exactly 0%
allocation can be high while goodput is low
fair queueing: B1 waits 1 slot instead of 10

retrieve.q: Explain why ‘unexplained waits feel longer’ matters for a scheduler, using the 64/46 case.
answer: with a bare status users invent a cause (a rival team, a bug)
they cancel and resubmit, usually losing their place
the numbers show the wait is physical: 18 GPUs are busy elsewhere

retrieve.q: Walk through how the card gets a mean utilization of 32.9% from the histogram, and why it's only approximate.
answer: take each bin's midpoint (0, 5, 15, … 95) times its share
approximate because every GPU in a bin is treated as sitting at its midpoint

retrieve.q: Finance's target is > 95% utilization. Argue why hitting it could still mean poor goodput, with the card's numbers.
answer: read the target as allocation: 95% of GPUs handed out
28% of allocated time at 0% leaves 0.95 × 0.72 = 68.4% doing any work
preempted-and-lost work lowers goodput further; track goodput and capacity waste

compare.q: The fair-share card divides capacity by entitlement; this card's fair queue orders waiting jobs round-robin by user. What does each guarantee, and how can each still feel unfair to a user?
answer: fair share: each user's slice over time, with idle capacity lent out
fair queue: no user's burst blocks another's next job
both can feel unfair without a visible reason: preemption back to entitlement, or a long wait behind a big gang job

compare.q: cs-5 separates yield and harvest from raw availability; this card separates goodput from utilization. What mistake does each distinction prevent?
answer: yield/harvest: counting a degraded answer as a full success
goodput: counting busy or allocated hardware as useful work
both: pick the metric the user experiences, not the one easiest to collect

predict.q: Under per-user round-robin, user A splits one big job into 10 tiny jobs to ‘get more turns’. Commit first: does A get more of the GPU? Would the answer differ under per-job round-robin?
predict.answer: Under per-user round-robin, no: each round gives A one slot however many jobs A queues, so splitting only changes A's own ordering. Under per-job round-robin, yes: A's 10 jobs would get 10 turns per round against B's 1. That's why fair queueing keys on the user (or team), not the job.

apply.task: One GPU, unit-length jobs. User A submits 4 jobs, then B submits 2, then C submits 1, all at once in that order. Write the start slot of every job under FCFS and under per-user round-robin, and the total waiting time for each. Check with fcfs and fair in code/scheduler-as-product.py. Then write the pending reason for a 64-GPU gang job with 60 free.
apply.done: FCFS: A0–A3 at 0–3, B0 4, B1 5, C0 6. Fair: A0 0, B0 1, C0 2, A1 3, B1 4, A2 5, A3 6. C's wait drops from 6 to 2 and A's last job's rises from 3 to 6; total wait is 0 + 1 + … + 6 = 21 slots in both, because fairness moves waiting, it doesn't remove it. Reason: PENDING (gang): needs 64 GPUs, 60 free, waiting for 4 more.
apply.hint: Round-robin takes the head of each user's queue in turn, dropping users whose queue is empty.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether splitting a job games the fair queue?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why total waiting time is the same under both queues?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: allocation → utilization, or utilization → goodput?
What would your own team's dashboard show if you replaced ‘GPUs allocated’ with goodput?
What will you look for in the order-book card: another system where priority and fairness are defined by a queue discipline?
